title: Adhesive Capsulitis (Frozen Shoulder)
case: Case: A 55-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes has 3 months of worsening left shoulder pain, worst at night, and cannot reach behind her back or comb her hair. Passive external rotation at the side is about 15 degrees on the left and 70 on the right. Passive abduction is also limited. Strength is normal apart from pain. X-ray is reported as normal.

Working diagnosis: adhesive capsulitis, probably in the freezing (painful) phase. Plan: education, gentle pain-guided mobility, sleep positioning, low-grade mobilization, discuss injection with the doctor, and a diabetes review with her doctor.

differentials.name: Glenohumeral osteoarthritis
differentials.key: Older age, grinding, joint space loss on X-ray

differentials.name: Locked posterior dislocation
differentials.key: Recent seizure, electric shock or fall; external rotation severely blocked

differentials.name: Calcific tendinopathy
differentials.key: Sudden severe pain, calcification on X-ray

qa: How do you separate frozen shoulder from a cuff problem on examination? Passive movement is limited in frozen shoulder, especially external rotation, whereas in cuff problems passive range is usually normal and the limit is pain on active movement.
Why avoid aggressive stretching in the painful phase? It may increase pain and inflammation and make the shoulder more irritable [Ref - to verify].
Why ask about a seizure or electric shock? These can cause a locked posterior dislocation that looks like a stiff shoulder and needs urgent imaging.
Why mention diabetes? It is a common association and may need medical review; blood sugar control may also matter [Ref - to verify].

The patient asks how long it will last. What do you say? Explain that the course is variable, from many months to a few years, with most people improving, and that treatment aims to reduce pain and keep as much function as possible [Ref - to verify].

tests.name: Passive external rotation at the side

fields.Purpose: Identify the key sign of frozen shoulder: large loss of passive external rotation
fields.Patient position: Supine or sitting, elbow at the side bent to 90 degrees
fields.Therapist position: Beside the patient, one hand stabilising the elbow, the other holding the wrist
fields.Action: Rotate the forearm outward slowly until firm resistance or pain stops it; use a goniometer if available; compare with the other side
fields.Positive: Clearly reduced passive external rotation compared with the other side, often with a firm end-feel. Some classification criteria use a loss of at least 50% of the other side [Ref - to verify exact criteria]
fields.Negative: Passive external rotation approximately equal to the other side
fields.Supports: Supports adhesive capsulitis, especially if other directions are also limited
fields.Limits: Also reduced in glenohumeral osteoarthritis and some dislocations; a normal X-ray helps separate them
fields.Errors: Allowing trunk lean or shoulder shrug; not stabilising the elbow; forcing past the end-feel
fields.Next step: If positive, check passive abduction and internal rotation, and refer for X-ray if arthritis or locked dislocation is possible

redFlags.Finding: Stiff shoulder after a seizure, electric shock or high-energy fall, with severely reduced external rotation
redFlags.Why it matters: Joint locked in the wrong position
redFlags.Immediate action: Do not mobilise; refer for imaging

redFlags.Finding: Constant severe night pain with weight loss, cancer history
Bilateral stiffness with morning stiffness, older age, fatigue, headache or jaw pain on chewing
redFlags.Immediate action: Refer same day if vision or headache involved

manual.name: Low-grade glenohumeral mobilization (painful phase)
manual.why: Short-term pain relief without forcing range
manual.finding: Irritable shoulder, high pain, night pain
manual.application: Supine, gentle oscillations in pain-free range, below the first resistance

manual.name: Graded mobilization to the end of range (stiff phase)
manual.application: Moderate-grade glides toward limited directions such as external rotation; short bouts
manual.stop: Pain over about 5 out of 10 or lasting into the next day

manualNotes: Preferred starting choice: education and symptom-guided gentle movement. Avoid aggressive stretching or forced end-range manipulation in the painful phase, because it can increase pain and may delay recovery [Ref - to verify]. The evidence for manual therapy in frozen shoulder is limited and mostly low in certainty [Ref - to verify]. Do not claim that mobilization breaks adhesions.
Is it working? Compare passive external rotation, night pain and function over weeks, not minutes. Natural recovery makes short-term judgments difficult.

exercise.Steps: Lean forward with support, let the arm hang and swing gently
exercise.Starting dose: 1 to 2 minutes, a few times daily

exercise.Exercise: Supine stick or towel external rotation
exercise.Steps: Lying, elbow at the side, push the hand outward with the other arm holding a stick
Seated, hands on a table, slide forward
Face the wall, walk fingers up

exerciseNotes: Dose idea: in the painful phase, use short, gentle, frequent movements below the pain threshold. In the stiff phase, use longer holds at the end of the available range, with mild to moderate stretch discomfort that eases within an hour [Ref - to verify].

modalities.name: Laser, shockwave
modalities.comment: Evidence limited and mixed [Ref - to verify]

modalityNotes: Medical options (decided by doctors): intra-articular corticosteroid injection, especially in the painful phase, which is reported to give short-term pain relief and some improvement in range [Ref - to verify]; hydrodilatation; manipulation under anaesthesia or arthroscopic capsular release for severe stiffness that does not improve. Timing is individual.
pathway: Emergency or urgent flag? Yes: act as in Section G.
Recent trauma, seizure or shock with locked rotation? Yes: refer urgently.
Passive external rotation clearly reduced in a capsular pattern, with pain and normal or non-explaining X-ray? Yes: working diagnosis is adhesive capsulitis.
Decide the phase from pain, night pain and stiffness.
If irritable and painful: calm first. If stiff and less painful: more active stretching.
If no progress or severe disability after months of care: medical review for injection or procedure options.
Visit 1: confirm the diagnosis and phase, screen flags, explain the usual course and that it improves with time.
Painful phase: pain control, sleep positioning, gentle movement, consider medical advice on injection.
